map.An Axiom City episode — Lessons 3-1 & 3-: An Axiom City episode — Lessons 3-1 & 3-2 at one time. It has three gates. Solve the math to move the story.
map.Race season status: ON. Training camp st: Race season: ON. Camp: 06:00. Crew: most of us are up.
map.Previously: on a rained-out field day, f: Last time: it rained on field day. Four sixth graders woke VEX in the old lab. VEX is a piece of Ada Vex's Pattern Engine. Now race season starts. The Courier Cup is a bike relay. It pays for the library. It is one week away. Camp opens at dawn.
map.The old depot lot, dawn. Bikes on the ra: The old bus lot, at dawn. Bikes on the rack. Paint on the table. Team Torque is there, watching.
map.Cute flag, junior leaguers. Torque's fla: Cute flag, kids. Torque's flag is gold. Like our trophies. Like our FUTURE.
map.It's not cute, Bram, it's a recipe: two: It is not cute, Bram. It is a recipe: two parts sky-blue to five parts white. Courier blue. I love this color.
The glitch for race day: high. Today: paint, pedals, and proportions. Mixing is math, crew. Get it wrong and the flag looks like chalk.
map.The paint table. One recipe card, many c: The paint table. One recipe card. Lots of cans. No room for mistakes.
map.A ratio, not a riddle: 2 cans of blue fo: A ratio, not a riddle: 2 cans of blue for every 5 of white. Say it like a beat: two FOR five.
map.The trim taught me the rule. Gray to amb: The trim taught me the rule. Gray to amber is 1 to 3. I doubled it once, 2 and 6. The shade did not change. Multiply BOTH numbers, or paint it all again.
map.Definition loaded: a ratio compares amou: Here is the rule: a ratio compares amounts. 1:3 is part-to-PART: gray against amber. The whole trim batch is 1 + 3 = 4 parts. So gray-to-WHOLE is 1:4. Same paint, two comparisons.
map.A ratio compares part to part (gray:ambe: A ratio compares part to part (gray:amber, 1:3). Or part to whole (gray:all the trim paint, 1:4). Scale a batch: multiply each part by the same number.
map.Reader — you're our fifth crew member. T: Reader, you are our fifth crew member. The flag needs a TRIPLE batch of Courier blue. Pour it right.
map.Courier blue is mixed 2 parts blue : 5 p: Courier blue is mixed 2 parts blue : 5 parts white. Chloe needs a TRIPLE batch for the flag. Fill the cans. Then answer one more question.
map.Then — in ANY batch of Courier blue, the: Then: take ANY batch of Courier blue. The ratio of blue to the TOTAL paint is:
map.Conceptual: a ratio keeps its color only: Conceptual: BOTH parts must scale the same. Only then does a ratio keep its color. A triple batch makes the WHOLE recipe three times. Look at a part-to-whole ratio. It compares one color to all the paint. Not to the other color.
map.Procedural: multiply each part of 2:5 by: Procedural: multiply each part of 2:5 by 3. Blue first, then white. Next question: add the recipe's parts (blue + white). That is the whole batch. Then write blue : whole.
map.The depot loop. Rohan has a stopwatch an: The bus loop. Rohan has a stopwatch and a clipboard. Juno is the new courier from Harbor Row. She wants to do her best.
map.Tryout logged! Chloe: 5.4 km in 18 minut: Tryout done! Chloe: 5.4 km in 18 minutes. Juno: 4.4 km in 11. Two riders. Not the same ride at all.
map.Shorter ride, I know. Don't read the odo: My ride was shorter, I know. Do not look at how far. Look at the stopwatch.
map.Definition loaded: a rate compares two d: Here is the rule: a rate compares two kinds of units. Here: kilometers AND minutes. Divide distance by time. That is the unit rate, km per ONE minute. One number per rider.
map.Like my warm-up: 2 km in 8 minutes. 2 ÷: Like my warm-up: 2 km in 8 minutes. 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 km a minute. The decimal does not care how long you rode.
map.A rate compares different units; a unit: A rate compares two kinds of units. A unit rate makes it "per one": km per 1 minute. Then two riders can be compared fairly.
map.Reader — run the division. Two unit rate: Reader, do the division. Two unit rates. One last leg. Who gets it?
map.Time-trial log: Chloe — 5.4 km in 18 min: Time-trial log: Chloe — 5.4 km in 18 min. Juno — 4.4 km in 11 min. Find each unit rate in km per minute. Then pick the anchor.
map.Conceptual: raw distance can't crown a r: Conceptual: how far alone can't pick a winner. The rides took different times. A unit rate: how far ONE minute takes each rider. Then any two rides compare fairly.
map.Procedural: divide distance by time — Ch: Procedural: divide distance by time. Chloe: 5.4 ÷ 18. Juno: 4.4 ÷ 11. Write each as a decimal of kilometers per minute. The bigger decimal goes more road each minute.
map.You benched the kid who rode FARTHEST? F: You left out the kid who rode FARTHEST? Farther means faster. Torque thanks you for the trophy.
map.Farther in MORE minutes, Bram. Speed is: Farther in MORE minutes, Bram. Speed is distance PER minute. The stopwatch wins each time.
map.Welcome to the crew, Juno. You bring the: Welcome to the crew, Juno. You bring the legs. The math brought the proof.
map.The supply shed, late afternoon. Race ru: The shed, late in the day. Race rule #12: each water stop has 3 bottles for each 2 riders.
map.Three bottles per TWO riders — so the or: Three bottles per TWO riders. So the order grows by rider-pairs. Count the pairs. Then give each pair its three bottles.
map.And pack prices are decoys. Boss math is: And pack prices can trick you. The real math is the price of ONE bottle. Divide the tag by the pack.
map.Demo from Kofi's juice run: a 6-pack for: Look at Kofi's juice run: a 6-pack for $7.20 → 7.20 ÷ 6 = $1.20 per bottle. The shelf tag is loud. The unit price tells the truth.
map.A unit price is a unit rate in dollars:: A unit price is a unit rate in dollars: cost ÷ count = price of ONE. Compare per-one prices. Never pack tags.
map.Sundown. The order form is due at the ra: Sundown. The form is due at the race office tonight. Bram leans on the door and smirks.
map.Torque's order took five minutes. Bet yo: Torque's order took five minutes. I bet your crew spends all the library's money. I bet you can't show the work.
map.Reader — three locks. Fill the form. Mak: Reader, three locks. Fill the form. Make each coin count.
map.Boss Gate: scale the 3:2 bottle ratio to: Boss Gate: scale the 3:2 bottle ratio to all riders. Price ONE bottle. Then pick the pack that saves the library's money.
BOSS GATE. Three locks. One smug rival. (No stress. Some stress.)
map.The race office form. 24 riders register: The race office form. 24 riders signed up. Each water stop has 3 bottles for every 2 riders. The shop sells bottles 5 for $7.50 or 4 for $6.40. Three locks:
map.Bulk pack: 5 bottles for $7.50. Price of: Big pack: 5 bottles for $7.50. Price of ONE bottle: $
map.Which pack is the better deal for the te: Which pack is the better deal for the team?
map.Conceptual: Lock 1 scales a ratio — 3:2: Conceptual: Lock 1 scales a ratio. 3:2 stays 3:2 for any number of riders. So think in groups of two riders. Locks 2 and 3 are unit prices. A pack tag means nothing. First know the cost of ONE bottle.
map.Procedural: Lock 1 — 24 riders ÷ 2 rider: Procedural: Lock 1: 24 riders ÷ 2 riders per group. Then 3 bottles for each group. Lock 2: divide $7.50 by 5. Lock 3: the 4-pack shows its per-bottle price. Compare it with Lock 2. Pick the cheaper bottle.
map.Nope. Division. You should try it before: Nope. Division. Try it before Saturday.
map.Camp's done. But race day feeds SIXTY vo: Camp is done. But race day feeds SIXTY helpers. We must scale all of Ms. Ortiz's recipe table.
map.New distortion humming at the main stage: A new glitch hums at the main stage. It grows in rows and columns. To be continued…
map.Ratio.2:5 means 2 of this for every 5 of: Ratio.2:5 means 2 of this for every 5 of that. Scale a batch: MULTIPLY both parts by the same number. Part-to-whole compares one part to all parts.
map.Rate & unit rate.A rate pairs two differ: Rate & unit rate.A rate pairs two units (km and minutes). Divide to get the per-ONE number: km per minute. Then riders can compare fairly at any distance.
Unit price.Cost ÷ count = price of one. The smaller per-one price is the better deal. The pack tag does not matter.
"Mix by multiplying. Judge by the unit. The city keeps its word in ratios." — A.V.
map.completed Unit 3 · Episode 1: Mix & Meas: beat Unit 3 · Episode 1: Mix & Measure. They know ratios, rates and unit rates. They know them well.
map.Thank you for riding with the crew. Epis: Thank you for riding with the crew. Episode 2 is being built now, in rows and columns.
map.Different bucket — banner paint, green:g: New bucket: banner paint, green:gold = 3:5. A DOUBLE batch multiplies both parts by 2 → 6 green, 10 gold. Same color. Bigger bucket.
map.Part-to-whole for that recipe: the bucke: Part-to-whole for that recipe: the bucket holds 3 + 5 = 8 parts. So green-to-whole is 3:8. That is green against ALL the paint.
map.The trap: adding the same number to both: The trap: adding the same number to both parts (4:6, 5:7…). It keeps the difference. But it ruins the color. Ratios scale by MULTIPLYING.
map.Your turn — same idea, different numbers: Your turn. Same idea, new numbers:
map.Banner paint is green:gold = 3:5. How ma: Banner paint is green:gold = 3:5. How many GOLD cans in a double batch?
map.Different tryout — scooters. Scooter A c: New tryout: scooters. Scooter A goes 4.5 km in 9 minutes: 4.5 ÷ 9 = 0.5 km per minute.
map.Scooter B covers 5 km in 25 minutes: 5 ÷: Scooter B goes 5 km in 25 minutes: 5 ÷ 25 = 0.2 km per minute. B went farther. But B is slower per minute.
map.Compare the per-minute decimals, not the: Compare the per-minute decimals, not the trip lengths. 0.5 beats 0.2. So A is faster, but its ride was shorter.
map.Scooter C covers 3 km in 6 minutes — wha: Scooter C goes 3 km in 6 minutes. What is its unit rate in km per minute?
map.Different shed — snack bars at 5 bars fo: New shed: snack bars at 5 bars for every 2 riders. For 8 riders: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 groups. Then 4 × 5 = 20 bars. Scale the ratio by groups.
map.Unit price: a 4-pack of bars costs $5.20: Unit price: a 4-pack of bars costs $5.20 → 5.20 ÷ 4 = $1.30 per bar.
map.Better deal: a 3-pack at $4.20 runs 4.20: Better deal? A 3-pack at $4.20 is 4.20 ÷ 3 = $1.40 per bar. So the 4-pack wins. It costs less PER BAR at any pack size.
map.One more 3-pack costs $3.90 — what is it: One more 3-pack costs $3.90. What is its price per bar?
map.Pour something first — both cans need a: Pour something first. Both cans need a number.
map.Those cans went in by ADDING — the same: Those cans went in by ADDING. The same extra for each color keeps the DIFFERENCE. It does not keep the ratio. A triple batch: multiply BOTH parts of 2:5 by the same number.
map.Not Courier blue yet. A triple batch mea: Not Courier blue yet. A triple batch is the whole 2:5 recipe, three times. Scale each part of it.
map.Cans are perfect! Now tag the follow-up: Cans are right! Now the next one: blue compared to the TOTAL paint.
map.2:5 compares blue to WHITE — part to par: 2:5 compares blue to WHITE. That is part to part. The next one asks: blue against ALL the paint.
map.That's the WHITE share of the bucket. Th: That is the WHITE share of the bucket. The next one asks about blue.
map.Order matters: that ratio reads total-to: Order matters. That ratio reads total-to-blue. Flip it.
map.Triple-true! 6 blue and 15 white still s: Triple-true! 6 blue and 15 white are still 2:5. A bucket holds 2 + 5 = 7 parts. So blue-to-total is 2:7. The flag dries a bright Courier blue.
map.Divide first — each rider needs a km-per: Divide first. Each rider needs a km-per-minute number.
map.Re-run the division: kilometers ÷ minute: Do the division again: kilometers ÷ minutes, one rider at a time. Keep it as a decimal.
Rates are done. Now pick the anchor.
map.Look again — 5.4 km is the longer RIDE,: Look again. 5.4 km is the longer RIDE. It is not the faster rider. Which decimal gets more road in one minute?
map.0.4 km per minute beats 0.3. Juno takes: 0.4 km per minute beats 0.3. Juno rides the last leg. The stopwatch never brags. It just divides.
map.Lock 1 first — the bottle count drives t: Lock 1 first. The bottle count drives the whole order.
map.Lock 1 holds. Flipped! 3 is the BOTTLE s: Lock 1 is shut. Flipped! 3 is the BOTTLE side of 3:2. Each group is 2 RIDERS. Count rider-pairs first.
map.Lock 1 holds. 12 is the number of rider-: Lock 1 is shut. 12 is the number of rider-PAIRS. Each pair still needs its 3 bottles.
map.Lock 1 holds. That would be 3 bottles pe: Lock 1 is shut. That is 3 bottles per ONE rider. The ratio says 3 per TWO riders.
map.Lock 1 holds. Split 24 riders into group: Lock 1 is shut. Split 24 riders into groups of 2. Then give each group its 3 bottles.
map.Lock 1 open! Lock 2: divide the pack pri: Lock 1 open! Lock 2: divide the pack price by the bottles in it.
map.Lock 2 holds. $7.50 split across 5 bottl: Lock 2 is shut. $7.50 split across 5 bottles. Divide, and keep the decimal.
map.Locks 1 and 2 open! Lock 3: compare the: Locks 1 and 2 open! Lock 3: compare the per-bottle prices. Pick a pack.
map.Lock 3 holds. $1.60 each is printed righ: Lock 3 is shut. $1.60 each is printed on the 4-pack. Lock 2 found ONE bottle's cost in the 5-pack. The smaller per-bottle price wins.
map.ALL LOCKS OPEN. 24 riders → 12 pairs → 3: ALL LOCKS OPEN. 24 riders → 12 pairs → 36 bottles. $7.50 ÷ 5 = $1.50 a bottle, and $1.50 beats $1.60. The 5-packs save the library's prize money. Order filed. Bram, hush.
Yes! Now go back and open that gate.
